Issued at 247 AM MDT Thu Aug 27 2026

An upper level high over has been rooted over the southwest CONUS 
over the past few days. The associated ridge axis is currently (230 
AM) positioned over far western Wyoming, where it has been for the 
past day or so. The ridge axis will begin to slowly shift east 
across Wyoming today and bring another day of widespread warm 
temperatures. With subtle height rises as the ridge progresses east, 
temperatures east of the Continental Divide are forecast to be in the 
high 80s to mid 90s. Western and southern Wyoming will likely see 
widespread highs in the 80s. However, today's forecasted highs 
across western Wyoming could be a few degrees too warm due to 
increased cloud cover this afternoon.

The increased cloud cover is a result of an influx of moisture with 
a shortwave disturbance on the upstream side of the ridge this 
afternoon and evening. Much like the past few days, showers and 
thunderstorms are expected to initiate across the higher terrain of 
western and southern Wyoming this afternoon and move east. Model 
forecast soundings are indicating DCAPE values ranging from 700 J/kg 
across western Wyoming to 1500 J/kg in central and southern Wyoming. 
Furthermore, dew point depressions across central and southern 
Wyoming are in the 45 to 55 degree range. Thus, another day of gusty 
outflows will be possible in any shower or thunderstorm across 
central and southern Wyoming late this afternoon. A couple gusts 
could be closer to that 55 to 60 mph mark, but most gusts will be in 
the 35 to 45 mph range. Unlike the past few days, shower and 
thunderstorm coverage is expected to be greatest across west and 
northwest Wyoming. This is due to those areas being in better 
proximity to the highest moisture content. Showers and thunderstorms 
are largely forecast from 1PM through at least 10PM, with light rain 
possible across the northern half of Wyoming until 2AM Friday.

By Friday, the upper level ridge will be positioned over the central 
CONUS, allowing for flow to be predominately southwesterly. This 
deep southwest flow will advect deep Pacific moisture into the 
region as embedded shortwaves traverse the state. Shower and a few 
embedded thunderstorms will be possible (up to 30% chance) as early 
as sunrise Friday across northwest Wyoming as the nose of the 
Pacific moisture arrives. These shower and thunderstorm chances will 
only increase through the day on Friday as a continuous stream of 
Pacific moisture advects into the state. Showers and thunderstorms 
are expected to initiate and be most numerous over the higher 
terrain in the afternoon and move east/northeast into the lower 
elevation areas. PWATs are expected to increase across the entire 
state through the afternoon and evening as southwest flow 
strengthens. Ensemble guidance indicates that PWATs will increase 
from the the 90th percentile of climatology in the morning to above 
the 99th percentile of climatology by Friday afternoon, especially 
across west and northwest Wyoming. This provides increased 
confidence in widespread showers and thunderstorms bringing at least 
a few hundredths of rain for many locations. The increased cloud 
cover across the state will also limit how warm we get on Friday, 
with forecasted highs in the 70s and 80s.

The active weather will continue Friday night through Saturday 
afternoon as a cold front traverses across the area. There will be 
plenty of available moisture, lift, and support aloft for widespread 
showers and thunderstorms. The highest chances (90%+) are still 
across the western half of Wyoming due to remaining in better 
proximity to the greatest moisture content. The current forecast has 
anywhere from 0.5" to 1.0" of rain between 6AM Friday through 
Midnight Sunday morning (42 hours) across Yellowstone, the Teton and 
Gros Ventre Mountains, the northern Wind River Mountains, and 
Jackson Valley. Amounts during this same timeframe elsewhere across 
the state range from 0.01" to 0.40". Showers and thunderstorms are 
not forecast to be slow moving. However, if multiple showers or 
thunderstorms with moderate to heavy rainfall rates go over the same 
area in a short amount of time, localized flash flooding is possible 
across west and northwest Wyoming. 

Showers and thunderstorms are expected to persist Saturday night 
through Sunday afternoon, although coverage will gradually decrease. 
This is decreasing trend will largely be a result of westerly flow 
cutting off the deeper moisture. Flow becomes more westerly and 
strengthens ahead of a shortwave trough rounding a Pacific Northwest 
low. This shortwave and an associated cold front is forecast to trek 
across the Intermountain West Sunday afternoon. This cold front is 
forecast to come with a "punch" of cold air, especially west of the 
Continental Divide. There is a 60% to 90% chance of temperatures on 
Monday morning falling into the 30s across the Green River Basin and
